Consumers, the frontend SPA, and federated remotes know **only** this API and the generated `@fuzefront/security-client` — never a vendor. We can switch or blend providers for features/cost without any consumer change. ## Naming rule (strict) No vendor/product name appears in ANY consumer-facing path, schema name, field, config key, or description. Open-standard protocol terms (OIDC/OAuth2/JWKS/PKCE) may appear where they describe a genuine wire protocol, but are kept out of consumer-facing **names** where practical. Provider names live only inside server-side adapter implementations and server-only environment configuration. ## Boundary guarantee For social login the user's browser only ever transits `app.fuzefront.com` and (briefly, for the chosen social provider) the provider's own consent host (e.g. `accounts.google.com`). No FuzeFront-internal identity host is ever visible to the browser or named in this contract. ## Broker (marketplace / consumer-product handoff) The `broker` tag is a DELIBERATE, narrower exception to the boundary guarantee above: a registered consumer product (e.g. the Mendys datasets marketplace, #238) sends its user to FuzeFront's OWN themed sign-in UI, and after authentication the browser is handed back to that product's own origin — never to any other, unregistered third party. The handoff never puts a bearer token in a URL, fragment, or referrer: only a single-use, short-lived opaque code (`POST /v1/security/broker/handoff`), redeemed by the product's BACKEND server-to-server (`POST /v1/security/broker/token-exchange`), exactly mirroring the existing `social/callback` → `session/exchange` code shape. This is a SEPARATE allowlist from the social broker's own `redirectTo` return-origin allowlist (#352), which governs FuzeFront's first-party social handshake, not this third-party handoff. ## Fail-closed Every AuthN and AuthZ decision is fail-closed: any verification, provider, or transport error yields a denial (401/403) or an explicit error body — never a permissive fallback. ## Delivery phasing AuthN is delivered first (it fixes the acute live provider leak); AuthZ is designed here in full and its consumer rollout is sequenced after AuthN. ## MFA + contact verification (provider-agnostic) Multi-factor step-up (`/mfa`) and contact-ownership verification (`/verify`, email + SMS) are provider-agnostic: internally they are backed by the identity provider's MFA stages and the family email/SMS services via the adapter, but consumers see only neutral factor `type` values (`totp`/`sms`/`email`, with room for `webauthn` later). license: name: MIT servers: - url: /api description: >- Same-origin API base. It exposes both authentication (AuthN) and authorization (AuthZ) behind a single, stable, same-origin contract under `/api/v1/security`. ## Provider-agnostic by design The underlying identity provider (federation / MFA / enrollment engine) and the authorization engine (policy / ReBAC) are **swappable implementations** hidden behind internal adapter interfaces (`IdentityProvider`, `AuthorizationProvider`). Consumers, the frontend SPA, and federated remotes know **only** this API and the generated `@fuzefront/security-client` — never a vendor. We can switch or blend providers for features/cost without any consumer change. ## Naming rule (strict) No vendor/product name appears in ANY consumer-facing path, schema name, field, config key, or description. Open-standard protocol terms (OIDC/OAuth2/JWKS/PKCE) may appear where they describe a genuine wire protocol, but are kept out of consumer-facing **names** where practical. Provider names live only inside server-side adapter implementations and server-only environment configuration. ## Boundary guarantee For social login the user's browser only ever transits `app.fuzefront.com` and (briefly, for the chosen social provider) the provider's own consent host (e.g. `accounts.google.com`). No FuzeFront-internal identity host is ever visible to the browser or named in this contract. ## Broker (marketplace / consumer-product handoff) The `broker` tag is a DELIBERATE, narrower exception to the boundary guarantee above: a registered consumer product (e.g. the Mendys datasets marketplace, #238) sends its user to FuzeFront's OWN themed sign-in UI, and after authentication the browser is handed back to that product's own origin — never to any other, unregistered third party. The handoff never puts a bearer token in a URL, fragment, or referrer: only a single-use, short-lived opaque code (`POST /v1/security/broker/handoff`), redeemed by the product's BACKEND server-to-server (`POST /v1/security/broker/token-exchange`), exactly mirroring the existing `social/callback` → `session/exchange` code shape. The redirect-URI allowlist enforcement, and the `BrokerClient` registration surface itself, are contract-frozen here but implemented as a follow-up (#238) — see the `broker` tag description. This is a SEPARATE allowlist from the social broker's own `redirectTo` return-origin allowlist (#352), which governs FuzeFront's first-party social handshake, not this third-party handoff. ## Fail-closed Every AuthN and AuthZ decision is fail-closed: any verification, provider, or transport error yields a denial (401/403) or an explicit error body — never a permissive fallback. ## Delivery phasing AuthN is delivered first (it fixes the acute live provider leak); AuthZ is designed here in full and its consumer rollout is sequenced after AuthN. ## MFA + contact verification (provider-agnostic) Multi-factor step-up (`/mfa`) and contact-ownership verification (`/verify`, email + SMS) are provider-agnostic: internally they are backed by the identity provider's MFA stages and the family email/SMS services via the adapter, but consumers see only neutral factor `type` values (`totp`/`sms`/`email`, with room for `webauthn` later). license: name: MIT servers: - url: /api description: >- Same-origin API base. Works identically under local TLS and prod ingress; never hard-code an absolute API host. tags: - name: session description: Session lifecycle — password login, current identity, logout, code exchange. - name: social description: Server-brokered social login. The browser never sees an internal identity host. - name: signup description: Server-brokered account creation. - name: broker description: >- Consumer-product sign-in handoff (marketplace token handoff, #238). A registered consumer product ("broker client") sends its user to FuzeFront's themed sign-in UI with `?client=&redirect_uri=`; after the user authenticates via the EXISTING `session`/`social`/`signup` surfaces, the product's backend redeems a single-use opaque code for a session — server-to-server, never a token in a URL, fragment, or referrer. Distinct from `social` (the social-provider handshake itself) and from `session.exchange` (FuzeFront's own first-party SPA session bootstrap): this tag is the THIRD-PARTY handoff surface, with its own redirect-URI allowlist per client, separate from #352's social-broker return-origin allowlist. `BrokerClient` registration (redirect-URI allowlist + `clientSecret` issuance) is contract-frozen here (`BrokerClient`, `BrokerTokenExchangeRequest`) but has no registration ENDPOINT in this slice — provisioning a broker client is an operator/platform-admin action tracked as a #238 follow-up. - name: capabilities description: Neutral capability descriptor for the auth surface. - name: authz description: >- Authorization decisions (check / bulk-check / permissions) + grants (write-side) + subject ABAC attribute writes (write-side data the provider's own policies read, distinct from a role/permission grant). - name: tenants description: Tenant, membership, and role management (neutralized authz primitives). - name: organizations description: >- Organization-tree surfaces. It exposes both authentication (AuthN) and authorization (AuthZ) behind a single, stable, same-origin contract under `/api/v1/security`. ## Provider-agnostic by design The underlying identity provider (federation / MFA / enrollment engine) and the authorization engine (policy / ReBAC) are **swappable implementations** hidden behind internal adapter interfaces (`IdentityProvider`, `AuthorizationProvider`). Consumers, the frontend SPA, and federated remotes know **only** this API and the generated `@fuzefront/security-client` — never a vendor. We can switch or blend providers for features/cost without any consumer change. ## Naming rule (strict) No vendor/product name appears in ANY consumer-facing path, schema name, field, config key, or description. Open-standard protocol terms (OIDC/OAuth2/JWKS/PKCE) may appear where they describe a genuine wire protocol, but are kept out of consumer-facing **names** where practical. Provider names live only inside server-side adapter implementations and server-only environment configuration. ## Boundary guarantee For social login the user's browser only ever transits `app.fuzefront.com` and (briefly, for the chosen social provider) the provider's own consent host (e.g. `accounts.google.com`). No FuzeFront-internal identity host is ever visible to the browser or named in this contract. ## Broker (marketplace / consumer-product handoff) The `broker` tag is a DELIBERATE, narrower exception to the boundary guarantee above: a registered consumer product (e.g. the Mendys datasets marketplace, #238) sends its user to FuzeFront's OWN themed sign-in UI, and after authentication the browser is handed back to that product's own origin — never to any other, unregistered third party. The handoff never puts a bearer token in a URL, fragment, or referrer: only a single-use, short-lived opaque code (`POST /v1/security/broker/handoff`), redeemed by the product's BACKEND server-to-server (`POST /v1/security/broker/token-exchange`), exactly mirroring the existing `social/callback` → `session/exchange` code shape. The redirect-URI allowlist enforcement, and the `BrokerClient` registration surface itself, are contract-frozen here but implemented as a follow-up (#238) — see the `broker` tag description. This is a SEPARATE allowlist from the social broker's own `redirectTo` return-origin allowlist (#352), which governs FuzeFront's first-party social handshake, not this third-party handoff. ## Fail-closed Every AuthN and AuthZ decision is fail-closed: any verification, provider, or transport error yields a denial (401/403) or an explicit error body — never a permissive fallback. ## Delivery phasing AuthN is delivered first (it fixes the acute live provider leak); AuthZ is designed here in full and its consumer rollout is sequenced after AuthN. ## MFA + contact verification (provider-agnostic) Multi-factor step-up (`/mfa`) and contact-ownership verification (`/verify`, email + SMS) are provider-agnostic: internally they are backed by the identity provider's MFA stages and the family email/SMS services via the adapter, but consumers see only neutral factor `type` values (`totp`/`sms`/`email`, with room for `webauthn` later). license: name: MIT servers: - url: /api description: >- Same-origin API base. It exposes both authentication (AuthN) and authorization (AuthZ) behind a single, stable, same-origin contract under `/api/v1/security`. ## Provider-agnostic by design The underlying identity provider (federation / MFA / enrollment engine) and the authorization engine (policy / ReBAC) are **swappable implementations** hidden behind internal adapter interfaces (`IdentityProvider`, `AuthorizationProvider`). Consumers, the frontend SPA, and federated remotes know **only** this API and the generated `@fuzefront/security-client` — never a vendor. We can switch or blend providers for features/cost without any consumer change. ## Naming rule (strict) No vendor/product name appears in ANY consumer-facing path, schema name, field, config key, or description. Open-standard protocol terms (OIDC/OAuth2/JWKS/PKCE) may appear where they describe a genuine wire protocol, but are kept out of consumer-facing **names** where practical. Provider names live only inside server-side adapter implementations and server-only environment configuration. ## Boundary guarantee For social login the user's browser only ever transits `app.fuzefront.com` and (briefly, for the chosen social provider) the provider's own consent host (e.g. `accounts.google.com`). No FuzeFront-internal identity host is ever visible to the browser or named in this contract. ## Broker (marketplace / consumer-product handoff) The `broker` tag is a DELIBERATE, narrower exception to the boundary guarantee above: a registered consumer product (e.g. the Mendys datasets marketplace, #238) sends its user to FuzeFront's OWN themed sign-in UI, and after authentication the browser is handed back to that product's own origin — never to any other, unregistered third party. The handoff never puts a bearer token in a URL, fragment, or referrer: only a single-use, short-lived opaque code (`POST /v1/security/broker/handoff`), redeemed by the product's BACKEND server-to-server (`POST /v1/security/broker/token-exchange`), exactly mirroring the existing `social/callback` → `session/exchange` code shape. The redirect-URI allowlist enforcement, and the `BrokerClient` registration surface itself, are contract-frozen here but implemented as a follow-up (#238) — see the `broker` tag description. This is a SEPARATE allowlist from the social broker's own `redirectTo` return-origin allowlist (#352), which governs FuzeFront's first-party social handshake, not this third-party handoff. ## Fail-closed Every AuthN and AuthZ decision is fail-closed: any verification, provider, or transport error yields a denial (401/403) or an explicit error body — never a permissive fallback. ## Delivery phasing AuthN is delivered first (it fixes the acute live provider leak); AuthZ is designed here in full and its consumer rollout is sequenced after AuthN. ## MFA + contact verification (provider-agnostic) Multi-factor step-up (`/mfa`) and contact-ownership verification (`/verify`, email + SMS) are provider-agnostic: internally they are backed by the identity provider's MFA stages and the family email/SMS services via the adapter, but consumers see only neutral factor `type` values (`totp`/`sms`/`email`, with room for `webauthn` later). license: name: MIT servers: - url: /api description: >- Same-origin API base. It exposes both authentication (AuthN) and authorization (AuthZ) behind a single, stable, same-origin contract under `/api/v1/security`. ## Provider-agnostic by design The underlying identity provider (federation / MFA / enrollment engine) and the authorization engine (policy / ReBAC) are **swappable implementations** hidden behind internal adapter interfaces (`IdentityProvider`, `AuthorizationProvider`). Consumers, the frontend SPA, and federated remotes know **only** this API and the generated `@fuzefront/security-client` — never a vendor. We can switch or blend providers for features/cost without any consumer change. ## Naming rule (strict) No vendor/product name appears in ANY consumer-facing path, schema name, field, config key, or description. Open-standard protocol terms (OIDC/OAuth2/JWKS/PKCE) may appear where they describe a genuine wire protocol, but are kept out of consumer-facing **names** where practical. Provider names live only inside server-side adapter implementations and server-only environment configuration. ## Boundary guarantee For social login the user's browser only ever transits `app.fuzefront.com` and (briefly, for the chosen social provider) the provider's own consent host (e.g. `accounts.google.com`). No FuzeFront-internal identity host is ever visible to the browser or named in this contract. ## Broker (marketplace / consumer-product handoff) The `broker` tag is a DELIBERATE, narrower exception to the boundary guarantee above: a registered consumer product (e.g. the Mendys datasets marketplace, #238) sends its user to FuzeFront's OWN themed sign-in UI, and after authentication the browser is handed back to that product's own origin — never to any other, unregistered third party. The handoff never puts a bearer token in a URL, fragment, or referrer: only a single-use, short-lived opaque code (`POST /v1/security/broker/handoff`), redeemed by the product's BACKEND server-to-server (`POST /v1/security/broker/token-exchange`), exactly mirroring the existing `social/callback` → `session/exchange` code shape. The redirect-URI allowlist enforcement, and the `BrokerClient` registration surface itself, are contract-frozen here but implemented as a follow-up (#238) — see the `broker` tag description. This is a SEPARATE allowlist from the social broker's own `redirectTo` return-origin allowlist (#352), which governs FuzeFront's first-party social handshake, not this third-party handoff. ## Fail-closed Every AuthN and AuthZ decision is fail-closed: any verification, provider, or transport error yields a denial (401/403) or an explicit error body — never a permissive fallback. ## Delivery phasing AuthN is delivered first (it fixes the acute live provider leak); AuthZ is designed here in full and its consumer rollout is sequenced after AuthN. ## MFA + contact verification (provider-agnostic) Multi-factor step-up (`/mfa`) and contact-ownership verification (`/verify`, email + SMS) are provider-agnostic: internally they are backed by the identity provider's MFA stages and the family email/SMS services via the adapter, but consumers see only neutral factor `type` values (`totp`/`sms`/`email`, with room for `webauthn` later). license: name: MIT servers: - url: /api description: >- Same-origin API base. It exposes both authentication (AuthN) and authorization (AuthZ) behind a single, stable, same-origin contract under `/api/v1/security`. ## Provider-agnostic by design The underlying identity provider (federation / MFA / enrollment engine) and the authorization engine (policy / ReBAC) are **swappable implementations** hidden behind internal adapter interfaces (`IdentityProvider`, `AuthorizationProvider`). Consumers, the frontend SPA, and federated remotes know **only** this API and the generated `@fuzefront/security-client` — never a vendor. We can switch or blend providers for features/cost without any consumer change. ## Naming rule (strict) No vendor/product name appears in ANY consumer-facing path, schema name, field, config key, or description. Open-standard protocol terms (OIDC/OAuth2/JWKS/PKCE) may appear where they describe a genuine wire protocol, but are kept out of consumer-facing **names** where practical. Provider names live only inside server-side adapter implementations and server-only environment configuration. ## Boundary guarantee For social login the user's browser only ever transits `app.fuzefront.com` and (briefly, for the chosen social provider) the provider's own consent host (e.g. `accounts.google.com`). No FuzeFront-internal identity host is ever visible to the browser or named in this contract. ## Broker (marketplace / consumer-product handoff) The `broker` tag is a DELIBERATE, narrower exception to the boundary guarantee above: a registered consumer product (e.g. the Mendys datasets marketplace, #238) sends its user to FuzeFront's OWN themed sign-in UI, and after authentication the browser is handed back to that product's own origin — never to any other, unregistered third party. The redirect-URI allowlist enforcement, and the `BrokerClient` registration surface itself, are contract-frozen here but implemented as a follow-up (#238) — see the `broker` tag description. This is a SEPARATE allowlist from the social broker's own `redirectTo` return-origin allowlist (#352), which governs FuzeFront's first-party social handshake, not this third-party handoff. ## Fail-closed Every AuthN and AuthZ decision is fail-closed: any verification, provider, or transport error yields a denial (401/403) or an explicit error body — never a permissive fallback. ## Delivery phasing AuthN is delivered first (it fixes the acute live provider leak); AuthZ is designed here in full and its consumer rollout is sequenced after AuthN. ## MFA + contact verification (provider-agnostic) Multi-factor step-up (`/mfa`) and contact-ownership verification (`/verify`, email + SMS) are provider-agnostic: internally they are backed by the identity provider's MFA stages and the family email/SMS services via the adapter, but consumers see only neutral factor `type` values (`totp`/`sms`/`email`, with room for `webauthn` later). license: name: MIT servers: - url: /api description: >- Same-origin API base. Consumers, the frontend SPA, and federated remotes know **only** this API and the generated `@fuzefront/security-client` — never a vendor. We can switch or blend providers for features/cost without any consumer change. ## Naming rule (strict) No vendor/product name appears in ANY consumer-facing path, schema name, field, config key, or description. Open-standard protocol terms (OIDC/OAuth2/JWKS/PKCE) may appear where they describe a genuine wire protocol, but are kept out of consumer-facing **names** where practical. Provider names live only inside server-side adapter implementations and server-only environment configuration. ## Boundary guarantee For social login the user's browser only ever transits `app.fuzefront.com` and (briefly, for the chosen social provider) the provider's own consent host (e.g. `accounts.google.com`). No FuzeFront-internal identity host is ever visible to the browser or named in this contract. ## Broker (marketplace / consumer-product handoff) The `broker` tag is a DELIBERATE, narrower exception to the boundary guarantee above: a registered consumer product (e.g. the Mendys datasets marketplace, #238) sends its user to FuzeFront's OWN themed sign-in UI, and after authentication the browser is handed back to that product's own origin — never to any other, unregistered third party. The redirect-URI allowlist enforcement, and the `BrokerClient` registration surface itself, are contract-frozen here but implemented as a follow-up (#238) — see the `broker` tag description. This is a SEPARATE allowlist from the social broker's own `redirectTo` return-origin allowlist (#352), which governs FuzeFront's first-party social handshake, not this third-party handoff. ## Fail-closed Every AuthN and AuthZ decision is fail-closed: any verification, provider, or transport error yields a denial (401/403) or an explicit error body — never a permissive fallback. ## Delivery phasing AuthN is delivered first (it fixes the acute live provider leak); AuthZ is designed here in full and its consumer rollout is sequenced after AuthN. ## MFA + contact verification (provider-agnostic) Multi-factor step-up (`/mfa`) and contact-ownership verification (`/verify`, email + SMS) are provider-agnostic: internally they are backed by the identity provider's MFA stages and the family email/SMS services via the adapter, but consumers see only neutral factor `type` values (`totp`/`sms`/`email`, with room for `webauthn` later). license: name: MIT servers: - url: /api description: >- Same-origin API base. ) } --- packages/security/openapi.yaml --- openapi: 3.1.0 info: title: FuzeFront Security API version: 0.9.0 description: >- The FuzeFront-owned, **provider-agnostic** Security API for the whole Fuze family. It exposes both authentication (AuthN) and authorization (AuthZ) behind a single, stable, same-origin contract under `/api/v1/security`. ## Provider-agnostic by design The underlying identity provider (federation / MFA / enrollment engine) and the authorization engine (policy / ReBAC) are **swappable implementations** hidden behind internal adapter interfaces (`IdentityProvider`, `AuthorizationProvider`). Consumers, the frontend SPA, and federated remotes know **only** this API and the generated `@fuzefront/security-client` — never a vendor. We can switch or blend providers for features/cost without any consumer change. ## Naming rule (strict) No vendor/product name appears in ANY consumer-facing path, schema name, field, config key, or description. Open-standard protocol terms (OIDC/OAuth2/JWKS/PKCE) may appear where they describe a genuine wire protocol, but are kept out of consumer-facing **names** where practical. Provider names live only inside server-side adapter implementations and server-only environment configuration. ## Boundary guarantee For social login the user's browser only ever transits `app.fuzefront.com` and (briefly, for the chosen social provider) the provider's own consent host (e.g. `accounts.google.com`). No FuzeFront-internal identity host is ever visible to the browser or named in this contract. ## Broker (marketplace / consumer-product handoff) The `broker` tag is a DELIBERATE, narrower exception to the boundary guarantee above: a registered consumer product (e.g. the Mendys datasets marketplace, #238) sends its user to FuzeFront's OWN themed sign-in UI, and after authentication the browser is handed back to that product's own origin — never to any other, unregistered third party. The handoff never puts a bearer token in a URL, fragment, or referrer: only a single-use, short-lived opaque code (`POST /v1/security/broker/handoff`), redeemed by the product's BACKEND server-to-server (`POST /v1/security/broker/token-exchange`), exactly mirroring the existing `social/callback` → `session/exchange` code shape. The redirect-URI allowlist enforcement, and the `BrokerClient` registration surface itself, are contract-frozen here but implemented as a follow-up (#238) — see the `broker` tag description. This is a SEPARATE allowlist from the social broker's own `redirectTo` return-origin allowlist (#352), which governs FuzeFront's first-party social handshake, not this third-party handoff. ## Fail-closed Every AuthN and AuthZ decision is fail-closed: any verification, provider, or transport error yields a denial (401/403) or an explicit error body — never a permissive fallback. ## Delivery phasing AuthN is delivered first (it fixes the acute live provider leak); AuthZ is designed here in full and its consumer rollout is sequenced after AuthN. ## MFA + contact verification (provider-agnostic) Multi-factor step-up (`/mfa`) and contact-ownership verification (`/verify`, email + SMS) are provider-agnostic: internally they are backed by the identity provider's MFA stages and the family email/SMS services via the adapter, but consumers see only neutral factor `type` values (`totp`/`sms`/`email`, with room for `webauthn` later). license: name: MIT servers: - url: /api description: >- Same-origin API base. Works identically under local TLS and prod ingress; never hard-code an absolute API host. tags: - name: session description: Session lifecycle — password login, current identity, logout, code exchange. - name: social description: Server-brokered social login. The browser never sees an internal identity host. - name: signup description: Server-brokered account creation. - name: broker description: >- Consumer-product sign-in handoff (marketplace token handoff, #238). A registered consumer product ("broker client") sends its user to FuzeFront's themed sign-in UI with `?client=&redirect_uri=`; after the user authenticates via the EXISTING `session`/`social`/`signup` surfaces, the product's backend redeems a single-use opaque code for a session — server-to-server, never a token in a URL, fragment, or referrer. Distinct from `social` (the social-provider handshake itself) and from `session.exchange` (FuzeFront's own first-party SPA session bootstrap): this tag is the THIRD-PARTY handoff surface, with its own redirect-URI allowlist per client, separate from #352's social-broker return-origin allowlist. `BrokerClient` registration (redirect-URI allowlist + `clientSecret` issuance) is contract-frozen here (`BrokerClient`, `BrokerTokenExchangeRequest`) but has no registration ENDPOINT in this slice — provisioning a broker client is an operator/platform-admin action tracked as a #238 follow-up. - name: capabilities description: Neutral capability descriptor for the auth surface. - name: authz description: >- Authorization decisions (check / bulk-check / permissions) + grants (write-side) + subject ABAC attribute writes (write-side data the provider's own policies read, distinct from a role/permission grant). - name: tenants description: Tenant, membership, and role management (neutralized authz primitives). - name: organizations description: >- Organization-tree surfaces.
